  --add-dir xdg-desktop \

There where multiple pieces that all came together.

Linux Mint ships p7zip-full by default, placing an old p7zip binary at `/usr/bin/7z`. When AppManager runs as an AppImage, the quick-sharun bundler restructures the internal layout from `/usr/bin` to `/bin`, so the bundled 7-Zip 25.01 ends up at $APPDIR/bin/7z. The old code resolved 7z using the compile-time path `/usr/bin/7z`, which on Mint found the host's p7zip instead of the bundled one and p7zip doesn't support -tSquashFS, causing E_NOTIMPL. 

On other distros there's typically no 7z on the host, so the lookup simply failed and fell through gracefully. The fix resolves 7z by looking next to the running executable via `/proc/self/exe`, which always finds the correct co-located bundled binary regardless of how the AppImage layout is restructured.

The upstream is the real problem.

GitHub releases are designed to hold variants of the same thing: different architectures, different package formats (.deb, .rpm, .AppImage), different OS targets. All of these are the same application in different containers.

DeltaChat is doing something unusual: publishing two fundamentally different applications (different toolkit, different runtime, different binary size, different feature set) under the same release tag. That's essentially two separate products sharing a release.

The proper upstream approach would be:

* Separate repos (deltachat-desktop + deltachat-tauri), or
* Separate release tags (desktop-v1.47.0 + tauri-v1.47.0)

A good examples would be [Bitwarden clients](https://github.com/bitwarden/clients/releases) that have Web, Desktop, Browser etc. all separated by the tags, but on the same repo. 

I could try to implement a fix with pattern-matching logic to handle this case, but that would be adding complexity to work around one project's unconventional release practice

Hi, I wanted to follow up on this because I don't think this behavior is harmless, and I just ran into another case where it actually broke things on my system.

I used AppManager to install the compiled AppImage from the releases page of [keychron_battery_widget](https://github.com/MrAdrianPl/keychron_battery_widget).

I later noticed that running python3 in my terminal was launching the Keychron AppImage instead of the actual Python interpreter. It also ended up breaking multiple apps and scripts running under my user that rely on python3 under the hood, because they kept triggering the AppImage instead of Python.

After digging around a bit, I've noticed that installing the AppImage creates a symlink at ~/.local/bin/python3 pointing to the AppImage binary. Since ~/.local/bin is often placed early in $PATH to prioritize user-installed binaries over system utilities, it completely hijacked the python3 command.

Here is what it looks like on my system:

```bash
liam@Corp:~$ whereis python3
python3: /usr/bin/python3 /usr/share/man/man1/python3.1.gz

liam@Corp:~$ Applications/AppManager install ./Downloads/KeychronBatteryWidget.AppImage 
Installed KeychronBatteryWidget

liam@Corp:~$ whereis python3
python3: /usr/bin/python3 /home/liam/.local/bin/python3 /usr/share/man/man1/python3.1.gz

liam@Corp:~$ file /home/liam/.local/bin/python3
/home/liam/.local/bin/python3: symbolic link to /home/liam/Applications/KeychronBatteryWidget
```

I really think there should be more hardened rules for how AppManager handles creating symlinks.

Besides breaking basic workflow tools, this is also a pretty big security risk. If a user installs an AppImage that happens to include internal binaries named after standard tools like python3, bash, git, or curl (whether it's just sloppy packaging or straight up malicious), those end up taking priority in ~/.local/bin/. That means any time the user or a local app tries to interact with Python or system utilities, it silently runs code from inside that AppImage instead.

A user shouldn't have to unpack and manually audit the internal structure of an AppImage before installing it just to make sure it won't break or hijack their system binaries.
